subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A rhyme scheme written as ABAB CDCD means...
options: The whole poem is one long sentence
Every line ends with the same word
There is no rhyme at all
Alternate lines rhyme within each quatrain
questions.explain: In ABAB the first and third, and second and fourth lines rhyme, creating an alternating pattern.

questions.q: Why might a writer use 'foreshadowing'?
options: To hint at events to come, building tension or a sense of inevitability
To confuse the reader about the genre
questions.explain: Foreshadowing plants clues about later events, creating suspense or a feeling that an outcome is unavoidable.

questions.q: Imagery that appeals to the senses (sight, sound, touch) is used by poets mainly to...
options: Make experiences vivid and draw the reader into the poem's world
questions.explain: Sensory imagery immerses the reader, making emotions and scenes feel concrete and immediate.

questions.q: In poems about 'nature', a common idea poets explore is...
options: Nature's power, beauty or indifference compared with human concerns
questions.explain: Nature poems often weigh human experience against nature's beauty, power or indifference to draw out a theme.

questions.q: A 'ballad' traditionally...
options: Has fourteen lines and a volta
Tells a story in regular, song-like stanzas, often with a refrain
questions.explain: Ballads are narrative poems in regular stanzas, often with a repeated refrain, rooted in oral storytelling.

questions.q: The 'protagonist' of a text is...
options: The central character whose journey drives the narrative
The character who opposes the hero
questions.explain: The protagonist is the main character at the centre of the action, often in conflict with an antagonist.

questions.q: To gain marks for using context, you should...
options: Link relevant context to how it shapes meaning or the reader's response
Retell the historical period in a separate paragraph
List as many dates as possible
questions.explain: Context earns credit when it illuminates the text's meaning or effect, not when it is merely recounted as history.

questions.q: 'Blank verse' is...
options: A stanza of exactly four lines
questions.explain: Blank verse is unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter, much used by Shakespeare for noble characters.

questions.q: A poem spoken in the voice of a single fictional speaker, revealing their character to a silent listener, is a...
questions.explain: A dramatic monologue uses one speaker's voice to expose their personality, often unintentionally, to an implied listener.

questions.q: A rhyming couplet at the end of a poem can be used to...
options: Indicate the poem is free verse
Provide a neat, emphatic sense of closure or a final twist
questions.explain: A closing couplet often rounds off the poem with a memorable, resolved or pointed final statement.

questions.q: If a poem's lines follow the pattern da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM, the metre is...
questions.explain: Five iambic feet per line is iambic pentameter, the most common metre in English poetry.

questions.q: A 'dramatic monologue' is especially useful for exploring 'power' because it...
options: Lets a single speaker reveal a controlling or arrogant character through their own words
questions.explain: By giving one speaker the floor, a dramatic monologue can expose their need for control or pride, sometimes unintentionally.

questions.q: How might 'sibilance' (repeated 's' sounds) be analysed in a poem?
options: It tells us the poet's age
It can create a soft, hissing or soothing sound that shapes mood
It proves the poem is a sonnet
questions.explain: Sibilance creates an audible texture, soft and hushed or sinister and snake-like, that an analyst connects to mood.

questions.q: A useful comparative connective to show contrast between two poems is...
questions.explain: Connectives like 'whereas', 'in contrast' and 'similarly' signal genuine comparison between the two poems' methods.

questions.q: When a writer uses an 'antagonist', this character mainly functions to...
options: Provide comic relief in every scene
Narrate events from a neutral standpoint
Oppose the protagonist and create conflict that drives the plot
questions.explain: The antagonist stands against the protagonist, generating the conflict that propels a narrative forward.

questions.q: If a poet writes in regular, controlled stanzas of equal length, an analytical reader might suggest this reflects...
options: A lack of effort by the poet
That the poem must be a ballad
Order, control or restraint that may mirror or contrast the poem's subject
questions.explain: Regular form can imply control or order, an effect a perceptive reader links to the poem's ideas or emotions.

questions.q: A 'sonnet' is most reliably identified by which feature?
options: Exactly three stanzas of six lines
Fourteen lines, usually in iambic pentameter, with a structured rhyme scheme
A refrain repeated after every stanza
questions.explain: The fourteen-line structure with a regular rhyme scheme and a turn is the hallmark of the sonnet form.

questions.q: The most analytical response to a striking image in an unseen poem is to...
options: Name the device, explore its effect, and link it to the poem's theme
State that the poet 'uses imagery' and move on
Skip it because it is unseen
questions.explain: Naming a method is only the start; exploring its effect and connecting it to meaning is what earns higher marks.

questions.q: When approaching an unseen poem, after grasping its meaning the next useful step is to...
options: Decide whether you like the poet personally
Compare it to a song on the radio
Examine HOW form, structure and language create that meaning
Memorise the poem word for word
questions.explain: Once the overall meaning is clear, analysing how methods build it turns understanding into developed analysis.

questions.q: A poem addressed directly to an absent person, abstract idea or object uses a device called...
questions.explain: Apostrophe is the direct address to someone absent or something non-human, often heightening emotional intensity.

questions.q: A 'semantic field' refers to...
options: The opening line of a play
A group of words linked by a shared area of meaning
questions.explain: A semantic field is a cluster of words relating to one theme, such as words of war or of disease, that shapes tone.

questions.q: When a poem about 'loss' uses the present tense to describe a person now gone, the effect is often to...
options: Keep the memory vivid and immediate, as if the person is still present
Prove the poem is a sonnet
Confuse the reader for no reason
questions.explain: Present tense can make memory feel alive and ongoing, emphasising how loss keeps the absent person emotionally present.
